bib.title: Code Generation with AlphaCodium: From Prompt Engineering to Flow Engineering

read.skipped: Figures (flow diagram, token-count screenshots) not viewed; text around them read.

question: Can a test-based, multi-stage, iterative code-oriented flow around an off-the-shelf LLM beat single-prompt engineering on hard competitive-programming problems without any fine-tuning?
hypothesis: Prompt-engineering tricks that work for natural language are not effective for code; running generated code against tests and iterating (with extra AI-generated tests) is more beneficial.
contributions: AlphaCodium: a test-based, multi-stage, code-oriented iterative flow (pre-processing phase plus code-iterations phase)
Code-oriented design concepts: YAML structured output, bullet-point analysis, modular code, soft decisions with double validation, postponed decisions, test anchors
Evaluation on CodeContests validation and test sets showing gains over direct prompts and over CodeChain/AlphaCode with far fewer LLM calls

method.summary: A flow (no training) around GPT-4, GPT-3.5 or DeepSeek-33B: reflect on the problem, reason on public tests, propose and rank 2-3 solutions, generate 6-8 extra AI tests, produce an initial code, then run-fix iterate on public tests and then on AI tests using test anchors. Compared with a single direct prompt on CodeContests with pass@5.

datasets.name: CodeContests validation
datasets.source: DeepMind CodeContests (Codeforces etc.); ~200 private tests per problem

inference.samples: pass@5: 5 generated solutions per problem; ~15-20 LLM calls per solution, ~100 calls per pass@5 submission; number of runs/seeds not stated
inference.prompting: Multi-stage prompts with YAML output matching Pydantic classes; bullet-point reflection; ask for modular code with small named sub-functions; direct-prompt baseline described only as 'a single well-designed direct prompt' (text not given)

parameters.initial_code_try_limit: a try-limit exists, value not stated
parameters.test_anchors: passed public tests become anchors; passing AI tests added; fixes must pass all anchors; AI tests sorted easy to hard
parameters.distance_for_failed_tests: L2 for numbers, sum of L2 for number arrays, count of differing cells for string arrays (Appendix D)

metrics.name: pass@k
metrics.definition: percentage of problems solved by using k generated solutions per problem (k=5)

metrics.name: pass@K@N (AlphaCode)
metrics.definition: N solutions generated and clustered, K submitted

eval.protocol: Private test set of ~200 tests per problem; comparisons to other works use numbers reported in their papers; no seeds, variance or significance reported.

results.claim: Fixed-code must pass accumulated test anchors, protecting against wrong AI tests
results.setup: Design rationale; no ablation of anchors reported

limits: No ablation of individual stages or design concepts (YAML, anchors, double validation, bullet points) is reported; only direct prompt vs full flow and a qualitative Fig 1b.
Model versions, temperature, max tokens, try-limits and iteration counts are not stated; direct-prompt baseline text is not given.
Single run per cell, no variance or significance reported; small eval sets (107 and 165 problems).
Comparisons to AlphaCode and CodeChain use their reported numbers, and the authors concede evaluation subtleties (multiple solutions, tolerance, timeouts); AlphaCode LLM call count is an assumption.
Appendix C lists tricks that did not help (execution trace of last 50 lines, last K failed solutions, last git patch diff, complicated single-stage prompts), with no numbers.
Only competitive programming evaluated; generalisation to other code tasks is asserted, not shown.
AlphaCode2 uses a separate unreleased CodeContests variant, so not comparable.

terms.definition: Tests (public ones, then AI-generated ones that passed) that any fixed code must also pass, so a wrong AI test cannot drive a bad fix
